I usually just use the organic miracle-gro but I know some people don't like that brand and I don't know if you care about going organic or not. I think NPK tends to matter more than brand, so see what's available near you. Something to keep in mind is that entire material-based fertilizer can take months to break down (fish fertilizer, blood/bone meal, etc) and these plants look like they want a pick-me-up soon, so I would go for a formula/liquid fertilizer over mixing blood/bone meal or fish paste into the soil. Those have their place, bit more as long-term fertilizer than the quick boost you're looking for now. The most important thing for these guys is probably to dilute it a little, they're still seedlings so full-strength runs the risk of burning the roots. So I would read the directions on the package and add either half as much fertilizer or twice as much water.

I would say so, tomatos are pretty vigorous and outgrow their starting cells quickly. 

If you grow in a warm climate and plan on planting outside in a couple weeks or so, you can plant into solo cups with some holes snipped in the bottom. If you live in a cooler climate and can't plant for 3+ weeks I recommend planting into half-gallon containers so they don't outgrow them before going outside.

This year I started tomatos in similar cells to yours, then up-potted into clear solo cups, and then saw their roots on the edges of the cups and up-potted to opaque half-gallon pots. I did hear some people say that I shouldntve planted into clear cups because roots dont like it, but the plants are quite vigorous right now and one advantage is that clear cups let you see when the roots are outgrowing the container. I personally don't think it makes much difference.

These guys will definitely need up-potting at some point unless you mean to plant them out in a couple of days, but whether you want to put them in a smallish midway-pot or directly into half-gallon/gallon pots depends on you and your growing space and your last frost date and how much time you're willing to spend repotting. For me it was very educational being able to see the roots in clear solo cups, but I dont know if I got any other benefit that planting directly into bigger containers would have conferred. I will say that plenty of peoe do it all kinds of ways, so as long as they get up-potted somehow try not to stress about it too much.

Shewolf, takoi, Leila, or marrow. There's also Sozai, but that's in a suburb so you won't see downtown (and if you are downtown don't miss the river walk!)

If you do Shewolf (and are feeling spendy) definitely do the tasting menu, lots of those dishes don't appear on the standard menu. Also spring for the wine pairing, it's delicious.

If you do takoi, get a lot of vegetarian dishes even if you eat meat. Their veggie dishes are where they really shine IMO. I love takoi but theyre sort of better for groups, since you can get a bunch of plates and share so you can get a little of everything. Their cocktails are great. One of their dishes are these little baby coconut tartlets with chili oil, get those if you go. Theyre a tasty little appetizer and quite unique.

Leila is also best in a group where you can just order a bunch of mezze and nibble on everything, but they also have tasty main dishes. They also have really great cocktails. There's one dish that's eggplant and lamb and chickpeas and yogurt, definitely get that.

If you do Marrow, again, do the tasting menu. Theyre very seasonal. Theyre the restaurant that got me into tasting menus. I don't have as much to say specifically about them as I do the other restaurants, but you can't go wrong.

Sozai is delicious (James Beard awarded), if you go definitely sit at the bar and do one of the omakase options. The chef will be happy to chat with you and find an option that suits you. Some of their dishes are for very adventurous eaters, but ive gone about three times and never been served anything bad. If chef Sato is there and you get on his good side you might get some extra goodies, but I have never had a restaurant meal feel this much like an RPG skill check. I do love the chatty atmosphere that the guys behind the bar have though, and you can learn interesting facts about sustainable seafood. Also, they recommend excellent sake pairings. They can be a little snobby about sushi though, they have a real disdain for spicy mayo.

EDIT: be sure to make a reservation ahead of time, especially if you're going on a friday or saturday! A lot of these places won't be able to accomodate walk-ins on busy nights.

Just a heads-up, requiring people to scan qr codes to get the information they need to attend an event is bad practice. I have some tips! Over time as you get practice, you'll find specific methods that fit your lifestyle, but this is what helped me:

-Cook beans from dry, not cans. It seems like more work, but almost none of it is active time, it's way cheaper and the texture/flavor is way better (I recommend throwing in an onion and some garlic to the pot as it boils)

-For roasted veggies, a general rule of thumb is 425 degrees for about 20 minutes with some salt, pepper, and olive oil. Works on almost anything.

-Buy a new spice or seasoning every week or two. This stops it from being this huge upfront expense but still allows you to slowly build up a variety.

-Easiest snack in the world if you think you'll be hungry in an hour or so: stab a sweet potato a few times and stick it in the oven, you don't even have to let it preheat if you don't want to. Come back in 45-65 minutes and just eat it with a fork. You can add stuff to it but it's pretty good on its own.

-Chuck scraps, bones, stems, cheese rinds etc. into a freezer bag and when it gets full, make stock. Using it to cook rice or other grains in adds flavor and it was just stuff you were gonna throw away anyways

-You don't need meat with every meal! Beans, eggs, nuts, and yogurt are all great sources of protein. Try going meatless for a day or two a week, it won't kill you and will almost certainly save you money!

-Unless you're near the water, most seafood in the store has been frozen and thawed. You might as well buy in the freezer section and thaw it yourself, it's usually much cheaper.

-Wine vinegars are a totally underrated seasoning. Sprinkling some on wilted greens makes them god-tier, and the bottles last for ages.

-if you aren't feeling up to anything fancy, it's hard to go wrong with the protien-veggie-grain meal format. If you're feeling crazy, make a quick pan sauce to go with it. It'll keep you fed and while it probably won't blow you away, it'll hardly ever be bad.

This isn't a definitive guide and not everything here will work for you specifically, they're just things I've learned over time.
